questions.question: Which description fits an integer linear program (ILP) as an optimization model with decision variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$?
options: A linear model in which every coefficient must be an integer.
A linear model in which some or all variables must be integers.
A model in which all variables must be integers and constraints may be nonlinear.
A linear model whose optimal value must turn out to be an integer.

questions.question: A transport model has decision variables for the number of buses hired, the litres of fuel bought, the hours of driver time and the kilometres driven. Which variable needs an integrality restriction?
options: The litres of fuel bought, since fuel is sold per litre.
The kilometres driven, since distances are counted in kilometres.
The hours of driver time, since wages are paid per hour.
The number of buses hired, as a bus cannot be split in two.

questions.question: A maximization LP has optimal value $z_{\mathrm{LP}}$. Integrality restrictions are then added to some variables, and the resulting ILP has optimal value $z_{\mathrm{IP}}$. Why does $z_{\mathrm{IP}}\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}$ hold?
options: Integer points always give smaller objective values than fractional points.
The ILP drops some constraints, so its feasible set becomes larger.
Each ILP-feasible point is LP-feasible, so the ILP searches fewer points.
Integer values are rounded down, so the objective value falls.

questions.question: In a model, a variable $x_j$ counting delivered pallets is restricted by $x_j\in\mathbb{Z}$ only. Which values does this allow?
options: All whole numbers, including negative ones such as $-3$.
All real numbers, since $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of reals.

questions.question: A planner solves an ILP by first ignoring the integrality restrictions and then rounding each variable of the fractional optimum to the nearest integer. What is the problem with this procedure?
options: Rounding always gives an infeasible point, so it can never be used.
Rounding changes the objective function, so values cannot be compared.
The rounded point may be infeasible, or feasible but not optimal.
Rounding is exact, but it takes longer than solving the ILP.

questions.question: For the ILP $\max\,5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$, the version without integrality has optimum $(3,1.5)$. Is the rounded-up point $(3,2)$ feasible for the ILP?
options: Yes, since both coordinates are integers.

questions.question: In a model with constraints $x_1+x_2\le4.5$, $x_2\le2.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, only $x_1$ must be an integer; $x_2$ is continuous. Which point is feasible?
A minimization model with cost $3x_1+5x_2$ has optimal cost 7.5 when the variables are continuous. Integrality is then required for both variables. What can be said about the new optimal cost $z$?
Consider the constraints $x_1+x_2\le2$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ with $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$. How many points does the feasible set contain?
A school must transport 130 pupils with buses of 40 seats each. With $x$ the number of buses, the model contains $40x\ge130$, $x\ge0$ and $x\in\mathbb{Z}$. What is the smallest feasible $x$?

For the ILP $\max\,3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$, the integer optimum is $(3,1)$. Why can its optimum not simply be found by checking the corner points of the continuous region?
options: The corners are always integer points, so checking them suffices.
The corners are fractional, so the objective cannot be evaluated.
The corner $(3.5,1.25)$ is optimal for the ILP as well.
The integer optimum $(3,1)$ lies strictly inside the region.

questions.question: An ILP is solved first without its integrality restrictions, and the optimal solution of this continuous version happens to have integer values for all integer-restricted variables. What follows for the ILP?
options: It is only a lower bound for a maximization ILP.
It is an optimal solution of the integer program too.
It must be rounded once more to confirm optimality.
It is feasible, but a better integer point may exist.

questions.question: Can adding integrality restrictions turn a linear program with a nonempty feasible region into a model with no feasible solution at all?
options: No, since integer points are a subset of the feasible region.
No, since every nonempty region contains an integer point.
Yes, if no point of the region has integer coordinates.
Yes, but only if the region is unbounded.

questions.question: With $x_1,x_2\ge0$ and $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$, which constraint allows exactly the same integer points as $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$?

For the ILP $\max\,5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$, the continuous version has optimal value 21 at $(3,1.5)$. Which value does integrality cost, i.e. continuous optimum minus integer optimum?
Solve $\min\,3x_1+5x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge2.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$. What is the optimal cost?
An ILP models whether to open a warehouse by a variable $w$ with $w\in\mathbb{Z}$. Which extra restriction makes $w$ a yes-or-no decision ($w=1$ open, $w=0$ closed)?
For $\max\,x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le3$, $2x_1\le3$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, a solver reports the continuous optimum $(1.5,1.5)$ with value 3. What happens when $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$ is added?
options: The value stays 3, attained for instance by the integer point $(1,2)$.
The value must drop below 3, since $(1.5,1.5)$ is not integer.
The model becomes infeasible, since $2x_1\le3$ has no integer solution.
The value rises above 3, since integer points are tighter.

questions.question: Solve the ILP $\max\,5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{Z}$. The continuous version has optimum $(3,1.5)$. Which point is the integer optimum?
For $\max\,5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, only $x_2$ must be an integer; $x_1$ stays continuous. What is the optimal value?
options: $20$, the value with both variables integer
$21$, the value with no integrality at all
